With XBLOCK=128, each CTA processes only 128 elements. The output store uses stride-832 (out_ptr0 + x0 + 832*x1), causing non-coalesced writes that stall warps waiting on L1TEX for 14.7 cycles on average (47.4% of all stall cycles). Increasing XBLOCK to 512, 1024, or 2048 via @triton.autotune will: (1) reduce the number of CTAs and launch overhead, (2) increase per-CTA work so the bias vector in_ptr1 (128 floats) is reused more from L1 cache, (3) allow the autotuner to find the tile size that best hides the strided-store latency through warp-level parallelism. With XBLOCK=512, the grid grows to 490 blocks giving ~3.7 waves for better SM saturation.

The 68.63% idle scheduler slots are driven by L1TEX stalls (47.4% of cycles) — more in-flight warps per SM from larger blocks help hide this latency. @triton.autotune will explore the optimal tile size automatically at runtime.

applicable_when: The kernel is a pointwise bias-add with a strided output (stride 832). It runs only 0.93 waves across 132 SMs. The dominant bottleneck is L1TEX scoreboard stalls (47.4% of all cycles, 14.7 cycles avg per stall), causing 68.63% scheduler idle slots. With XBLOCK=128 and only 4 warps per CTA, there are insufficient in-flight warps to hide memory latency. Three prior attempts to fix this via XBLOCK autotuning all failed correctness because the index decomposition x0 = xindex % 128 / x1 = xindex // 128 is hardcoded to the channel dimension (128), so any XBLOCK that is not exactly 128 causes incorrect x0/x1 values and out-of-bounds strided stores. The safe fix is to increase num_warps from 4 to 8 via autotune, keeping XBLOCK=128 unchanged.
